summary:
Earth Jukebox is an interactive web experience that pairs NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) visuals with sound, making Earth science explorable through both sight and hearing. Visitors can explore nine themes—including sea level change, air quality, disasters, water resources, agriculture, biodiversity, wildfires, greenhouse gases, and energy—and discover place-based environmental stories across the Philippines. Sonification translates visual patterns and, where available, time-series data into changing pitch and harmonics, while charts, descriptions, and source references provide context for what the data show and what they cannot.

The project matters because important Earth science is often presented visually, leaving fewer ways to engage with it. Sound offers an additional route for exploration, including for people who are blind or have low vision, and can make patterns easier to notice. By connecting NASA visualizations with local stories and clearly identifying data sources, scale, and limitations, Earth Jukebox aims to make planetary science more engaging without overstating what the measurements mean.
details:
Earth Jukebox is an interactive web and mobil application that lets people explore Earth science through maps, NASA visualizations, data stories, and sound. It was created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge Earth Jukebox challenge, with a focus on environmental stories from the Philippines.

HOW IT WORKS

Visitors begin at an interactive globe, choose an Earth-science theme, and explore mapped places and their stories. Each story combines a chart and explanatory context with a soundscape generated from its environmental time series. Playback follows the selected data over time: normalized values shape synthesized audio, and users can explore the timeline month by month.

The application also provides a dedicated NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) listening experience across nine themes. It pairs each theme with a cited NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) image, extracted video frames, or animation. The browser samples image pixels using an offscreen canvas: brightness influences pitch, while color variation influences harmonic content. For animations and frame sequences, the sound responds as the imagery advances; for still images, a scan moves across the image. This is an artistic sonification of visual features, not a direct reading of every underlying scientific measurement.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Earth science is often communicated visually. Adding sound creates another way to explore patterns and makes the experience more multisensory, including for people who are blind or have low vision. Charts, written descriptions, captions, and source links provide visual and textual context alongside audio. By connecting NASA visualizations with Philippine place-based stories, Earth Jukebox aims to make complex environmental topics more approachable, encourage curiosity about Earth-observation data, and support conversations about local and global change.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

The browser application uses React 19 and TypeScript, built with Vite. Web Audio API synthesizes the sound; HTML Canvas analyzes visual frames; MapLibre GL JS presents the interactive globe. Story observations are bundled as JSON so the experience does not need to fetch its time-series data from NASA while a visitor explores. Python scripts support offline data retrieval and processing, with tests for data-pipeline behavior. The project runs in a modern web browser on desktop or mobile; no specialized hardware is required.

CREATIVE APPROACH AND FACTORS CONSIDERED

The project combines scientific exploration with musical interpretation: users can listen to both a NASA visualization and a separate, place-based data story, then compare what each communicates. The sound mappings are intentionally designed to be exploratory and engaging rather than presented as scientific units or predictions.

Scientific scope and transparency guide the experience. Each visualization and story identifies its source, time period, geographic scale, and important limitations. Global or model-based imagery is not described as a Philippine observation. Satellite proxies are not presented as direct measurements of ground-level pollution, crop yield, biodiversity, electricity access, or disaster damage. Missing observations remain missing rather than being treated as zero; any short-gap estimates are distinguished from measured values. Non-NASA sources are identified where used. The application is an independent educational project, not an official NASA product.

SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI) DISCLOSURE

Generative AI assisted with drafting project and submission descriptions and implementing the SI disclosure in the About page. The app's scientific datasets and NASA visuals are sourced and documented, not AI-generated. Its audio is synthesized algorithmically from image features and data, not generated by AI.
